decks.title: Plant Kingdom — Part 1: Algae and bryophytes
goals: Compare green, brown and red algae and list the uses of algae
Describe liverworts and mosses and draw the life cycle of Funaria
Explain alternation of generations with the dominant gametophyte of bryophytes

slides.heading: Plant Kingdom
slides.body_md: Part 1 — from simple algae to the first land plants.

visual.alt: Flow from algae through bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms to angiosperms, in order of increasing body complexity

slides.narration: Plants range from microscopic algae to giant trees. Botanists group them by body organisation, by whether vascular tissue is present, and by whether seeds are formed. In this part we study the algae and the bryophytes, the groups without vascular tissue.

slides.heading: What are algae?
slides.body_md: Algae are simple, **chlorophyll-bearing, thalloid** autotrophs. They have no true root, stem or leaf and no vascular tissue.

rows: Thallus: unicellular, colonial, filamentous or leaf-like
Fresh water, sea water, moist soil and rocks
Mostly single-celled, without a protective jacket

visual.alt: Table of general features of algae

slides.narration: An alga has a thallus, a body that is not differentiated into root, stem and leaf. It may be a single cell, a colony or a long filament. Most algae live in water, and all of them make food by photosynthesis, so they are producers in aquatic food chains.

slides.heading: A brown alga: body plan
slides.body_md: Large brown algae show the most elaborate thallus: a **holdfast** that anchors the plant, a **stipe**, and a leaf-like **frond** that may carry **air bladders** to keep it afloat.

slides.narration: The holdfast fixes the alga to a rock but does not absorb water the way a root does. The stipe lifts the frond towards the light. Each part of the body can absorb minerals directly from the sea water, and the air bladders help the frond to float.

slides.heading: Green, brown and red algae compared
slides.body_md: The three classes differ in pigments, stored food, cell wall, flagella and habitat.

rows: Cellulose with an outer gel of algin
Cellulose with pectin and polysulphate esters

visual.alt: Table comparing the pigments, stored food, cell wall, flagella, habitat and examples of green, brown and red algae

slides.narration: Green algae have the same chlorophylls as land plants and store starch. Brown algae carry a brown pigment called fucoxanthin and store mannitol and laminarin, and their walls are coated with a gel called algin. Red algae have the red pigment phycoerythrin, store floridean starch and never form flagellate cells.

slides.heading: How algae reproduce
slides.body_md: Reproduction is **vegetative** (fragmentation), **asexual** (zoospores; non-motile spores in red algae) and **sexual** (isogamous, anisogamous or oogamous).

rows: A filament breaks into fragments, each growing into a new thallus
Flagellated zoospores formed in sporangia; red algae form non-motile spores
Large non-motile egg fuses with a small motile male gamete

visual.alt: Table of vegetative, asexual and sexual reproduction in algae with examples

slides.narration: Algae reproduce in three ways. A filament may simply fragment. Many form motile zoospores. In sexual reproduction the gametes may look alike, or differ in size, or be an egg and a small swimming male cell. Red algae have no motile cells, so their spores and male gametes are carried by the water.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the class
slides.body_md: A rocky-shore collection has 60 algae: 18 green, 27 brown and 15 red. Find what share is brown and how many have flagellate cells.
bullets: Brown share = 27 out of 60, which is **45 percent**.
Red algae never form flagellate cells, so only the green and brown algae can: 18 + 27 = **45**.
A specimen with phycoerythrin and floridean starch must be a red alga; one with fucoxanthin and mannitol, a brown alga.

visual.alt: Table matching diagnostic clues to the class of alga

slides.narration: First turn the counts into a share: twenty-seven brown algae out of sixty is forty-five percent. Next use the rule that red algae never have flagella, so only the green and the brown ones can; that gives forty-five. Pigments and stored food are the surest clues to the class.

slides.heading: Quick check: pigments
slides.body_md: Which class of algae is identified by phycoerythrin and floridean starch?
slides.narration: Quick check. The red pigment gives the name of the class.

slides.heading: Economic importance of algae
slides.body_md: Algae fix about **half of the carbon dioxide** used on Earth, and many are useful to people.

rows: Base of aquatic food chains; releases oxygen

visual.alt: Table of economic uses of algae

slides.narration: Algae supply a large share of the oxygen we breathe and form the base of food chains in the sea. People eat some seaweeds, extract agar from red algae and algin from brown algae, and use Chlorella as a protein-rich supplement.

slides.heading: Bryophytes: liverworts and mosses
slides.body_md: Bryophytes are **amphibians of the plant kingdom**: they live on land but need water for fertilisation. They have **rhizoids**, no true roots and no vascular tissue.

rows: Two stages: creeping protonema, then an upright leafy stem
Fragmentation and budding of the secondary protonema

visual.alt: Table comparing liverworts and mosses

slides.narration: Bryophytes are small plants of damp places. They lack xylem and phloem, so they cannot grow tall. Liverworts have a flat thallus that often forms little gemma cups. Mosses have a protonema stage followed by an upright leafy shoot.

slides.heading: A moss plant
slides.body_md: The green, leafy **gametophyte** is the dominant, haploid plant. The **sporophyte** — foot, seta and capsule — stays attached to it and gets water and food from it.

slides.narration: Start at the spore. It germinates into a creeping protonema, which grows into the leafy plant. Antherozoids swim in a film of water to the egg in the archegonium. The zygote grows into a sporophyte, and meiosis in its capsule gives new haploid spores.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: spores and chromosomes in a moss
slides.body_md: An imagined moss has 12 chromosomes in each gametophyte cell, and each capsule holds 250 spore mother cells.
bullets: Sporophyte cells are diploid: 2 × 12 = **24** chromosomes.
Each spore mother cell gives four spores by meiosis: 250 × 4 = **1000** spores.
Each spore is haploid, so it carries **12** chromosomes.

visual.alt: Table of ploidy and chromosome numbers at each moss stage

slides.narration: The sporophyte is diploid, so double the gametophyte number. Meiosis turns each spore mother cell into four haploid spores, so two hundred and fifty mother cells give one thousand spores, each with the haploid number of chromosomes.

slides.heading: Quick check: spores
slides.body_md: How many spores would a capsule with 125 spore mother cells release?
slides.narration: Quick check. Each mother cell divides by meiosis.

slides.heading: Quick check: moss stages
slides.body_md: Which stage of the moss life cycle grows directly from a germinating spore?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a creeping, thread-like stage.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Algae: chlorophyll-bearing thalloid autotrophs; green (starch), brown (mannitol, algin) and red (floridean starch, no flagella).
Uses: food, agar, algin, carrageen, Chlorella as single-cell protein, oxygen and food-chain base.
Bryophytes: liverworts and mosses; rhizoids; need water for fertilisation; dominant gametophyte.
Funaria: spore, protonema, leafy gametophyte, gametes, zygote, sporophyte (foot, seta, capsule), meiosis, spores.
Sporophyte of a bryophyte is dependent on the gametophyte.

visual.alt: Summary table of the dominant generation in algae and bryophytes

slides.narration: To recap: algae are simple chlorophyll-bearing plants grouped by pigments into green, brown and red, with many economic uses. Bryophytes are small land plants whose haploid gametophyte dominates and whose sporophyte depends on it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In an algae table, always give **pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella** for each class.
Draw the life cycle as a graphic outline and **mark n and 2n** at every stage.
Write that the moss sporophyte is **attached to and dependent on** the gametophyte.
Name the product with the organism: **agar from Gelidium**, **algin from brown algae**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Compare the classes on pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella. Mark the chromosome number at every stage of a life cycle. State clearly that the moss sporophyte depends on the gametophyte. And pair every product with its alga.

decks.title: Plant Kingdom — Part 2: Pteridophytes and gymnosperms
goals: Name the four classes of pteridophytes and distinguish homospory from heterospory
Draw the life cycles of a fern and of Pinus
Compare gymnosperms with pteridophytes and state their economic importance

slides.heading: Vascular plants without flowers
slides.body_md: Part 2 — ferns and their allies, and the naked-seeded plants.

visual.alt: Flow from bryophytes to pteridophytes to gymnosperms, showing sporophyte dominance and seed formation

slides.narration: Pteridophytes are the first plants with xylem and phloem, so they can grow tall. Gymnosperms go one step further and keep their spores inside ovules, which become naked seeds. In both groups the sporophyte is the dominant plant.

slides.heading: Pteridophytes: four classes
slides.body_md: Pteridophytes have **true roots, stems and leaves** with **xylem and phloem**, but **no seeds**. Their sporophyte is dominant.

rows: Simplest living vascular plants, no true roots
Jointed stem with whorled scale leaves

visual.alt: Table of the four classes of pteridophytes with examples

slides.narration: The four classes are Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida and Pteropsida. Psilotum is the simplest. Selaginella and Lycopodium belong to the club mosses, Equisetum is the horsetail, and the ferns such as Dryopteris are in Pteropsida.

slides.heading: Life cycle of a fern
slides.body_md: The leafy **sporophyte** bears **sporangia in sori**. Spores give a small, heart-shaped, free-living **prothallus** bearing antheridia and archegonia; the zygote grows into a new sporophyte.

slides.narration: The fern plant you see is the diploid sporophyte. Spore mother cells in sporangia divide by meiosis. The spore grows into a tiny prothallus, the haploid gametophyte. Antherozoids need water to reach the egg. The zygote then develops into a new fern plant.

slides.heading: Sporophyte and gametophyte of a fern
slides.body_md: Both generations are **independent and photosynthetic** in a fern, but the sporophyte is much larger.

visual.alt: Table comparing the sporophyte and the prothallus of a fern

slides.narration: The fern sporophyte makes spores by meiosis. The prothallus makes gametes by mitosis, because it is already haploid. Unlike a moss, the fern sporophyte is independent of the gametophyte once it has established itself.

slides.heading: Homospory and heterospory
slides.body_md: Most pteridophytes are **homosporous**; a few — **Selaginella, Salvinia, Marsilea** — are **heterosporous**.

rows: Male from microspore, female from megaspore

visual.alt: Table comparing homosporous and heterosporous pteridophytes

slides.narration: In homosporous plants all spores look alike and give one kind of gametophyte. Heterosporous plants make small microspores and large megaspores. In Selaginella the female gametophyte stays inside the megaspore wall, which is a step towards the seed.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting fern spores
slides.body_md: A fern sporangium has 16 spore mother cells. A sorus has 40 sporangia and a frond has 30 sori. The sporophyte has 48 chromosomes.
bullets: Spores per sporangium: 16 × 4 = **64**.
Spores per sorus: 64 × 40 = **2560**.
Spores per frond: 2560 × 30 = **76800**.
Each spore, and the prothallus, has 48 ÷ 2 = **24** chromosomes.

visual.alt: Worked table of fern spore numbers and chromosome count

slides.narration: Sixteen spore mother cells make sixty-four spores. Multiply by the number of sporangia in a sorus, then by the number of sori on a frond. The huge total shows how many spores one fern can release. Each spore is haploid, so it has half the number of chromosomes of the sporophyte.

slides.heading: Economic importance of pteridophytes
slides.body_md: Pteridophytes are used as ornamentals, as biofertiliser and as a source of coal in the geological past.

Grows on loose soil and stabilises it

visual.alt: Table of economic uses of pteridophytes

slides.narration: Many ferns are grown as ornamental plants. Azolla grows with a nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium and is added to paddy fields as a green manure. Giant ferns of ancient forests were buried and slowly turned into coal.

slides.heading: Gymnosperms: naked seeds
slides.body_md: **Gymnos** means naked: the **ovules are not enclosed in an ovary**, so the seeds are exposed. Most are woody trees or shrubs, and none forms flowers or fruits.

rows: Tap roots; mycorrhiza in Pinus; coralloid roots with cyanobacteria in Cycas
Unbranched in Cycas; branched in Pinus, Cedrus
Needle-like in conifers; pinnate in Cycas

visual.alt: Table of characteristics of gymnosperms

slides.narration: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds on cones. They are heterosporous, forming microspores that become pollen grains and megaspores that stay inside ovules. Conifer leaves are needles with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata, which reduces water loss.

slides.heading: Life cycle of Pinus
slides.body_md: The **tree is the dominant sporophyte**. **Pollen** from male cones is carried by wind; one **functional megaspore** in each ovule forms the **female gametophyte**; the **pollen tube** delivers the male gametes.

The pollen tube grows to the archegonium, and fertilisation gives a zygote that becomes the embryo inside a naked seed. No water is needed for fertilisation.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: ovules and pollen in a pine
slides.body_md: A female pine cone has 60 scales with 2 ovules each. A male cone has 500 pollen mother cells.
bullets: Each ovule has one megaspore mother cell giving 4 megaspores: 120 × 4 = **480**, of which **120** are functional.
Pollen grains: 500 × 4 = **2000**.

visual.alt: Worked table of ovules, megaspores and pollen grains in Pinus

slides.narration: Count the ovules first, one hundred and twenty. Each has one megaspore mother cell, giving four megaspores, but only one survives, so there are one hundred and twenty functional megaspores. Pollen is made in far greater numbers, two thousand from five hundred mother cells, because wind pollination is wasteful.

slides.heading: Gymnosperms compared with pteridophytes
slides.body_md: Gymnosperms have moved a step beyond ferns: **seeds, pollen tubes and a reduced gametophyte**.

visual.alt: Table comparing pteridophytes and gymnosperms

slides.narration: A fern needs water for its antherozoids to swim, and its gametophyte lives on its own. A gymnosperm keeps its gametophytes inside the sporophyte, uses wind-borne pollen and a pollen tube, and so fertilisation does not depend on water.

slides.heading: Economic importance of gymnosperms
slides.body_md: Gymnosperms supply **timber, resin, paper pulp and medicines**.

visual.alt: Table of economic uses of gymnosperms

slides.narration: Conifers give softwood timber and resin, from which turpentine is made. The stem of Cycas yields sago starch. Ephedra gives the drug ephedrine, and the bark of yew trees gives taxol, used in cancer treatment.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Pteridophytes: Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida, Pteropsida; vascular, no seeds; sporophyte dominant; prothallus free-living.
Homosporous (Dryopteris) and heterosporous (Selaginella, Salvinia): heterospory leads towards the seed habit.
Fern: 16 spore mother cells give 64 spores per sporangium.
Gymnosperms: naked seeds, cones, heterosporous, pollen tube, no water needed; Pinus life cycle.
Uses: ornamentals, Azolla biofertiliser; timber, resin, sago, ephedrine, taxol.

slides.narration: To recap: pteridophytes are vascular plants that reproduce by spores, with a dominant sporophyte and a free-living prothallus. Gymnosperms are woody, heterosporous plants with naked seeds, a reduced gametophyte and fertilisation by a pollen tube.

sections.heading: 1. Algae: Chlorophyceae, Phaeophyceae and Rhodophyceae
sections.body_md:
**Algae** are simple, chlorophyll-bearing, autotrophic organisms with a **thallus**: no root, stem or leaf and no vascular tissue. They may be unicellular (*Chlamydomonas*), colonial (*Volvox*), filamentous (*Ulothrix*, *Spirogyra*) or large and leaf-like (kelps). They live in fresh water, sea water, on moist soil and on rocks. Their sex organs are mostly single-celled and have no sterile jacket.

**The three classes** are separated by pigments, stored food, cell wall, flagella and habitat (see the table). In **brown algae** the body is differentiated into a **holdfast**, a **stipe** and a **frond**; in *Sargassum* and similar algae air bladders keep the frond afloat. **Red algae** have the pigment **phycoerythrin** and no flagellated cell at any stage, so their spores and male gametes are carried passively by water.

**Reproduction** is **vegetative** (fragmentation of the thallus), **asexual** (by flagellated **zoospores** in green and brown algae, non-motile spores in red algae) and **sexual** (fusion of gametes). The gametes may be similar (**isogamous**, as in *Ulothrix*), dissimilar in size (**anisogamous**, as in *Eudorina*) or an egg and a small motile male gamete (**oogamous**, as in *Volvox* and *Fucus*).

**Economic importance.** Algae carry out about half of the total carbon dioxide fixation on Earth and release oxygen; they are the primary producers of aquatic food chains. *Porphyra*, *Laminaria* and *Sargassum* are eaten as seaweed. **Agar**, used in laboratories and in food, comes from *Gelidium* and *Gracilaria* (red algae); **algin** from brown algae and **carrageen** from red algae are thickening agents; *Chlorella* and *Spirulina* are rich in protein and are grown as **single-cell protein**; and *Chlorella* is a possible food supplement for space travel.

*Where books differ.* Some books list five or more uses; the five above are the ones usually asked. The "about half of the carbon dioxide fixation" figure is the one given in standard textbooks and is approximate.

sections.heading: 2. Bryophytes: liverworts and mosses; the life cycle of Funaria
sections.body_md:
**Bryophytes** are small, mostly terrestrial plants of damp, shaded places, called the **amphibians of the plant kingdom** because they live on land but need water for fertilisation. The plant body is thalloid or leafy, attached by **rhizoids**, and has **no xylem or phloem**. The main plant body is the haploid **gametophyte**.

**Liverworts** (*Marchantia*, *Riccia*) have a flat, dorsiventral thallus; *Marchantia* reproduces asexually by **gemmae** formed in **gemma cups**. **Mosses** (*Funaria*, *Polytrichum*, *Sphagnum*) have two stages: a creeping, green, branched **protonema** that grows directly from the spore, and the upright **leafy gametophyte** that develops from it, with spirally arranged leaves and rhizoids.

**Life cycle of Funaria (graphic outline).** Haploid **spore** → **protonema** → **leafy gametophyte** (dominant) bearing **antheridia** (making **antherozoids**) and **archegonia** (each with an egg) at the shoot tips → antherozoids swim in a film of water to the egg → **zygote** (diploid) → **sporophyte** with **foot, seta and capsule**, which stays attached to the gametophyte and depends on it for water and food → in the capsule **spore mother cells divide by meiosis** to give haploid **spores**, released when the lid (operculum) opens and the peristome teeth bend.

**Alternation of generations.** A haploid gametophyte (gamete-forming) alternates with a diploid sporophyte (spore-forming). In bryophytes the **gametophyte is dominant** and the sporophyte is short-lived and dependent; in pteridophytes and gymnosperms the sporophyte is dominant.

**Economic importance.** *Sphagnum* gives **peat**, used as fuel, and its great water-holding capacity makes it a packing material for transporting live plants and a soil conditioner in horticulture. Mosses grow on bare rock and soil, form mats that bind the soil and reduce erosion, and are pioneers of **ecological succession**.

*Where books differ.* Some books describe the *Funaria* sex organs as on separate branches of one plant (monoecious); others mention only the apex of the main shoot and its branch. Either wording earns the marks provided that antheridia and archegonia are both named.

sections.heading: 3. Pteridophytes: classes, fern life cycle, homospory and heterospory
sections.body_md:
**Pteridophytes** are the first land plants with **true roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)**, but they do not form seeds. They are found in cool, damp, shaded places. The main plant body is the **sporophyte**, which bears **sporangia** on leaf-like **sporophylls**; in ferns the sporangia are grouped in **sori** on the underside of the leaves (fronds).

**Four classes with examples**
- **Psilopsida:** *Psilotum* (and the fossil *Rhynia*).
- **Lycopsida:** *Lycopodium*, *Selaginella*.
- **Sphenopsida:** *Equisetum*.
- **Pteropsida:** *Dryopteris*, *Pteris*, *Adiantum* (ferns); *Marsilea*, *Salvinia* (water ferns).

**Fern life cycle (graphic outline).** Sporophyte (2n) → spore mother cells in sporangia → **meiosis** → haploid **spores** → spore germinates into a small, green, heart-shaped, free-living **prothallus** (the gametophyte, n) with **antheridia** and **archegonia** on its lower surface → antherozoids swim in water to the egg → **zygote** (2n) → young sporophyte. Fertilisation needs water. In a typical leptosporangiate fern each sporangium has 16 spore mother cells and gives 64 spores.

**Homospory and heterospory.** Most pteridophytes are **homosporous**, producing one kind of spore (*Dryopteris*, *Lycopodium*, *Equisetum*). *Selaginella*, *Salvinia* and *Marsilea* are **heterosporous**, producing small **microspores** and large **megaspores**; they give male and female gametophytes respectively. In *Selaginella* the female gametophyte develops inside the megasporangium and the young embryo is nourished by it: the beginning of the **seed habit**.

**Economic importance.** Ferns such as *Adiantum* and *Nephrolepis* are ornamental; *Azolla* shelters the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterium *Anabaena* and is a biofertiliser in paddy fields; *Equisetum* helps to bind loose soil; and giant fern-like plants of the Carboniferous period formed coal deposits.

sections.heading: 4. Gymnosperms: characteristics and the life cycle of Pinus
sections.body_md:
**Gymnosperms** are plants whose **ovules are not enclosed in an ovary**, so the seeds are **naked**; they form no flowers or fruits. They include tall trees (*Pinus*, *Cedrus*, redwood), shrubs and cycads (*Cycas*). Roots are tap roots; those of *Pinus* have **mycorrhiza** and those of *Cycas* have **coralloid roots** with cyanobacteria. The stem is unbranched in *Cycas* and branched in *Pinus* and *Cedrus*. Leaves are needle-like in conifers, with a thick cuticle and sunken stomata that reduce water loss, and pinnate in *Cycas*. All are **heterosporous**: **microspores** form pollen grains in **microsporangia** on microsporophylls and **megaspores** form in **ovules** on megasporophylls, arranged in **cones**. The male and female gametophytes are reduced and do not live independently.

**Life cycle of Pinus (graphic outline).** The tree is the dominant **sporophyte**. In the male cone, **pollen mother cells** divide by **meiosis** to give **microspores**, which develop into winged **pollen grains** (the male gametophyte). In the female cone each ovule has a **megaspore mother cell** that divides by meiosis into **four megaspores**; **one is functional** and develops into the **female gametophyte** with **archegonia**, the other three degenerate. Wind carries pollen to the ovule (**pollination**); a **pollen tube** carries the male gametes to the egg, so **water is not needed**. Fertilisation takes place long after pollination (many months in *Pinus*); the **zygote** forms the **embryo**, the ovule becomes a **seed**, and the seed germinates into a new tree.

**Gymnosperms and pteridophytes compared.** Gymnosperms form **seeds**, are always **heterosporous**, retain a **reduced gametophyte** within the sporophyte, and do not need water for fertilisation because of the pollen tube; pteridophytes have no seeds, are mostly homosporous, have a free-living prothallus and need water.

**Economic importance.** Softwood **timber** (*Pinus*, *Cedrus*); **resin** from which turpentine and rosin are obtained (*Pinus*); **sago** starch from the stem of *Cycas*; **ephedrine** from *Ephedra*; **taxol** from *Taxus*; paper pulp; and ornamental trees such as *Thuja* and *Araucaria*.

*Where books differ.* The interval between pollination and fertilisation in *Pinus* is given as about a year in many books; "many months to over a year" is safe wording. Taxol is obtained from the bark of the yew (*Taxus*).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving only the colour of an alga class; the marks are for pigments, stored food, cell wall and flagella.
- Forgetting to mark **n** and **2n** (and meiosis) on a graphic outline of a life cycle.
- Saying that the moss sporophyte is independent; it is attached to and dependent on the gametophyte.
- Writing that all pteridophytes are heterosporous (most are homosporous).
- Saying that gymnosperms have fruits; they have naked seeds.
- Treating a prothallus as a sporophyte; it is the haploid gametophyte.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a term, an example, a stored food, a pigment, ploidy of a stage, a give-a-reason.
- 2- and 3-mark questions: tables of differences, three examples with uses, short life-cycle descriptions.
- 5-mark questions in parts: a graphic outline of the Funaria, fern or Pinus life cycle with labels, then a comparison and a reason.

live on land but need water for the antherozoids to swim to the egg

options.text_md: They are pioneers of succession that bind particles and add organic matter

questions.solution_md: Mosses form mats, trap soil particles and prepare the substratum — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sporophyte of Funaria remains attached to the gametophyte throughout its life.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but meiosis in the capsule does not explain why the sporophyte stays attached; the foot absorbing water and food does — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Bryophytes do not grow to a large size.

answer.model_answer_md: They have **no xylem or phloem**, so water and food cannot be carried over long distances.

questions.stem_md: State two economic uses of Sphagnum.

answer.model_answer_md: **Peat** from Sphagnum is used as **fuel**. Because it can hold a great deal of water, it is used to **pack and transport live plants** and as a **soil conditioner** in horticulture.

questions.solution_md: Two uses.

questions.stem_md: During a long dry spell no young sporophytes appear on a moss clump growing on a garden wall, although its gametophytes are healthy. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: The **antherozoids are flagellated** and must **swim through a film of water** from the antheridium to the egg in the archegonium. In dry weather no water film forms, so **fertilisation fails** and **no zygote or sporophyte** develops.

questions.solution_md: Flagellated antherozoids need a water film.

marking_scheme.step: Antherozoids swim and need a water film

questions.stem_md: Which generation is dominant in Funaria? State two ways in which the sporophyte depends on it.

answer.model_answer_md: The **gametophyte** (haploid leafy plant) is dominant. The sporophyte **remains attached** to it by its **foot**, and receives **water and mineral salts** and **food** from it.

questions.solution_md: Gametophyte; dependence.

marking_scheme.step: Foot absorbs water, minerals and food from the gametophyte

answer.model_answer_md:
| Feature | Liverworts | Mosses |
|---|---|---|
| Gametophyte | Flat, dorsiventral thallus | Protonema, then an upright leafy axis |
| Asexual reproduction | Gemmae in gemma cups | Budding of the secondary protonema |
| Example | Marchantia | Funaria |

The examples are named in the last row.

questions.solution_md: Three differences with examples.

questions.stem_md: Describe three ecological or economic roles of bryophytes.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Sphagnum** gives **peat**, a fuel, and holds water for packing plants.
2. Mosses grow on bare rock and soil and **bind the soil**, reducing **erosion**.
3. They are **pioneers of succession**, adding organic matter so that larger plants can follow.

questions.solution_md: Three roles.

questions.stem_md: Starting from the zygote, describe how the sporophyte of Funaria develops and how it releases spores.

answer.model_answer_md: The **diploid zygote** divides to form an embryo that grows into the **sporophyte** with a **foot, seta and capsule**. The foot is embedded in the gametophyte. In the capsule **spore mother cells** divide by **meiosis** to give **haploid spores**, released when the lid opens.

questions.solution_md: Zygote to spores.

marking_scheme.step: Zygote grows into foot, seta, capsule

questions.stem_md: What is alternation of generations? Explain how it differs in a moss and in a fern.

answer.model_answer_md: It is the **alternation of a haploid gametophyte** (forming gametes) **with a diploid sporophyte** (forming spores). In a **moss** the gametophyte is **dominant** and the sporophyte depends on it; in a **fern** the sporophyte is **dominant** and the small prothallus is free-living.

questions.solution_md: Definition and the contrast.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a graphic outline of the life cycle of Funaria, marking the haploid and diploid stages. [3]
(b) Which generation is dominant? [1]
(c) Name the process by which spores are formed and the structure in which it occurs. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Spore (n)** → **protonema (n)** → **leafy gametophyte (n)** with **antheridia** and **archegonia** → **antherozoid (n)** + **egg (n)** → **zygote (2n)** → **sporophyte (2n)** of foot, seta and capsule → **spore mother cells (2n)** → meiosis → spores (n).

(b) The **gametophyte** (leafy plant) is dominant.

(c) **Meiosis**, in the **capsule** of the sporophyte.

questions.solution_md: Outline with ploidy; dominant generation; meiosis in the capsule.

questions.solution_md: Such retention and nourishment of the embryo foreshadow the seed — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What is heterospory? Name two pteridophytes that show it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Heterospory** is the formation of **two kinds of spores**, small **microspores** and large **megaspores**, which give male and female gametophytes. **Selaginella** and **Salvinia** (also Marsilea) are heterosporous.

questions.solution_md: Definition and examples.

marking_scheme.step: Two kinds of spores, micro and mega

questions.stem_md: Describe the gametophyte of a fern and say why it needs a damp habitat.

answer.model_answer_md: It is a small, green, **heart-shaped, free-living prothallus** of **haploid** cells, bearing **antheridia** and **archegonia** on the lower surface. It needs **water** because the **antherozoids are flagellated** and swim to the egg.

questions.solution_md: Features and water.

marking_scheme.step: Heart-shaped haploid prothallus with sex organs

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which pteridophytes are useful to human beings.

answer.model_answer_md: Ferns such as **Adiantum** and **Nephrolepis** are grown as **ornamentals**. **Azolla** with **Anabaena** is used as a **biofertiliser** that adds nitrogen to paddy fields. (Giant ferns of the past also formed **coal**.)

questions.solution_md: Two uses.

questions.stem_md: Name any three classes of pteridophytes, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Psilopsida**: *Psilotum*.
2. **Lycopsida**: *Lycopodium* or *Selaginella*.
3. **Sphenopsida**: *Equisetum*.
(The fourth class, **Pteropsida**, includes *Dryopteris*, *Pteris* and *Adiantum*.)

questions.solution_md: Three classes and examples.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish homosporous from heterosporous pteridophytes on the spores, the gametophytes and one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Homosporous** pteridophytes form **one kind of spore**, which grows into a **bisexual, free-living gametophyte** (*Dryopteris*). **Heterosporous** ones form **microspores** and **megaspores**, which give **male and female gametophytes** (*Selaginella*). In heterosporous plants the female gametophyte may be retained in the sporangium, an advance towards the seed habit.

questions.solution_md: Three contrasts.

marking_scheme.step: Spores: one kind vs two kinds

questions.stem_md: Describe the sporophyte of a fern and explain where its spores are produced and by what division.

answer.model_answer_md: The **sporophyte** is a diploid plant with a **rhizome, roots and large compound leaves (fronds)**. The sporangia are in **sori** on the lower surface of the fronds. Inside each sporangium **spore mother cells** divide by **meiosis** to form **haploid spores**.

questions.solution_md: Body; sori; meiosis.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a graphic outline of the life cycle of a fern, marking n and 2n and the point of meiosis. [3]
(b) Is a fern homosporous or heterosporous? Define the term you choose. [1]
(c) Why does fertilisation in a fern need water? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Sporophyte (2n)** → **spore mother cells (2n)** in sporangia of sori → **meiosis** → **spores (n)** → **prothallus (n)** with **antheridia** and **archegonia** → **antherozoids (n)** and **egg (n)** → **zygote (2n)** → young sporophyte.

(b) A fern such as Dryopteris is **homosporous**: it forms only **one kind of spore**.

(c) The **antherozoids are flagellated** and must **swim** in water to the egg in the archegonium.

questions.solution_md: Outline; homospory; water.

one haploid megaspore and three polar bodies
two pollen grains and two eggs

questions.solution_md: Megaspores formed = 120 × 4 = 480; functional 120; degenerate 480 − 120 = 360.

answer.model_answer_md: Their **ovules are not enclosed by an ovary**, so the seeds are **not covered by a fruit**.

questions.stem_md: On a dry mountain slope pine trees set abundant seed, whereas ferns grow only in the damp ravines. Which feature of the pine explains this? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: The **pollen tube** carries the **male gametes directly to the egg**, so fertilisation **does not depend on water**, whereas fern antherozoids must **swim in water** to reach the egg. This lets the pine reproduce on **dry land**.

questions.solution_md: Pollen tube, no water needed.

marking_scheme.step: No need for water, unlike ferns

questions.stem_md: Name two products obtained from gymnosperms and the plant that gives each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sago** comes from the stem of **Cycas**; **resin**, from which turpentine and rosin are made, comes from **Pinus**. (Taxol is obtained from **Taxus** and ephedrine from **Ephedra**.)

questions.solution_md: Two products with plants.

questions.stem_md: State three characteristic features of gymnosperms, with an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **ovules are naked**, not enclosed in an ovary, and no **fruits or flowers** form.
2. They are **heterosporous**, bearing **microspores and megaspores** on sporophylls grouped in **cones**.
3. The **gametophytes are reduced**, and a **pollen tube** delivers the male gametes. Examples: *Pinus*, *Cycas*.

questions.solution_md: Three features.

questions.stem_md: Gymnosperms show advances over pteridophytes. State three such advances.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Gymnosperms form **seeds**; pteridophytes do not.
2. Their **female gametophyte stays within the ovule** instead of living freely as a prothallus.
3. A **pollen tube** removes the need for **water** in fertilisation. They are also **always heterosporous**, whereas most pteridophytes make only one kind of spore, so their sexes are separated earlier in the life cycle.

questions.solution_md: Seeds, retained gametophyte, pollen tube.

questions.stem_md: Describe what happens to the megaspore mother cell in a pine ovule until the archegonia are formed.

answer.model_answer_md: The **megaspore mother cell** (diploid) divides by **meiosis** to form **four haploid megaspores**. **Three degenerate**; the **one functional megaspore** grows into the **female gametophyte**, which develops **archegonia**, each with an egg. The female gametophyte is retained within the ovule and is nourished by the sporophyte.

questions.solution_md: Meiosis; one functional; female gametophyte.

questions.stem_md: A pine tree produces far more pollen grains than ovules. Give three facts about its pollination that explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Pollination is by **wind**, so most pollen never reaches a cone. The pollen grains are **winged**, which helps them float, but many are lost. Producing **very large numbers** of pollen grains therefore ensures that **some reach the ovules**; the loss of the rest is the price of not needing water or an animal carrier.

questions.solution_md: Wind pollination, wastage, numbers.

marking_scheme.step: Winged grains lost in the air
Large numbers ensure some reach the ovule

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a graphic outline of the life cycle of Pinus showing the sporophyte, the two kinds of cones, the spores and the fertilisation. Mark n and 2n. [3]
(b) How many of the four megaspores formed in an ovule survive? [1]
(c) Name the generation that is dominant and state one way in which it differs from the dominant generation of a moss. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Pine tree (2n)** → **male cone**: pollen mother cells (2n) → meiosis → **pollen grains (n)**, winged; **female cone**: ovule with **megaspore mother cell (2n)** → meiosis → **functional megaspore (n)** → **female gametophyte (n)** with **archegonia** → egg; **pollen tube** → **fertilisation** → **zygote (2n)** → **embryo** in a **naked seed**.

(b) **One** survives; three degenerate.

(c) The **sporophyte** is dominant. In a moss the **gametophyte** is dominant and the sporophyte is dependent; in Pinus the sporophyte is a **tall independent tree**.

questions.solution_md: Outline; one megaspore; dominant sporophyte.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Cones, spores and fertilisation in order

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name one homosporous and one heterosporous pteridophyte. [1]
(b) Compare pteridophytes and gymnosperms in four ways. [3]
(c) Why is Selaginella regarded as a step towards the seed habit? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Dryopteris** (homosporous) and **Salvinia** (heterosporous).

(b) **Seeds:** absent in pteridophytes, naked in gymnosperms. **Spores:** mostly homosporous vs always heterosporous. **Gametophyte:** free-living prothallus vs reduced, retained. **Water for fertilisation:** needed vs not needed.

(c) In **Selaginella** the **female gametophyte stays inside the megasporangium** and nourishes the young embryo.

questions.solution_md: Examples; four comparisons; Selaginella.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Four comparisons (three marks: four, three, or two)

questions.solution_md: The seta belongs to the diploid sporophyte: 2 × 12 = 24.

questions.passage_md:
A class collected five plants on a field trip and recorded what they saw.

| Specimen | Observation |
|---|---|
| P | Brown, slimy; holdfast, stipe and flat frond; stores mannitol |
| Q | Flat, ribbon-like green thallus with gemma cups |
| R | Heart-shaped green plate on damp soil under a fern, 5 mm across |
| S | Large tree with needles and cones; ovules lie bare on the scales |
| T | Feathery plant with sori on the underside of its fronds |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) R

**(b)** (b) P, Q and R

**(b)** P is an alga, Q a liverwort and R the prothallus of a fern, a gametophyte; none has vascular tissue. S and T are sporophytes with xylem and phloem — option (b).

**(c)** Group and difference.
